Which of the following statements regarding quadratic forms are true?

I. $R(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}$ is positive-definite

II. $S(x)={x}^{T}\,[\begin{aligned}-6 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]x$ is indefinite

III. $T(x)=-{x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{2}^{2}$ is negative-definite
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that, a quadratic form $Q(x)$ is:

- positive-definite if $Q(x)>0$ for all $x\in {R}^{n}∖\{0\};$

- negative-definite if $Q(x)<0$ for all $x\in {R}^{n}∖\{0\};$

- indefinite if 

- $Q({x}_{1})>0$ for some ${x}_{1}\in {R}^{n},$ and

- $Q({x}_{2})<0$ for some ${x}_{2}\in {R}^{n}.$

With that in mind, let's examine each of the quadratic forms in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, since

$$
\begin{aligned}R(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}>0\end{aligned}
$$

for all $x\in {R}^{n}∖\{0\},$ the quadratic form is positive-definite.

- Statement II is true. Substituting ${x}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S({x}_{1}) & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-6 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =2>0,\end{aligned}
$$

while substituting ${x}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S({x}_{2}) & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-6 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-4<0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the quadratic form is indefinite.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, since

$$
\begin{aligned}T(x)=-{x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{2}^{2}<0\end{aligned}
$$

for all $x\in {R}^{n}∖\{0\},$ the quadratic form is negative-definite.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

questions.problem:
Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}].$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. The eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=5$

II. ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ is positive-definite

III. $A$ is indefinite
questions.worked_solution:
Given a quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}Ax,$ we have the following theorem:

- $Q$ is positive-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are positive,

- $Q$ is positive semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-negative (note that positive semi-definite quadratic forms include all positive-definite quadratic forms),

- $Q$ is negative-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are negative,

- $Q$ is negative semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-positive (note that negative semi-definite quadratic forms include all negative-definite quadratic forms), and

- $Q$ is indefinite if and only if $A$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Computing the characteristic equation of $A,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )(3-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +5 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =1,\,5.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true, while statement III is false. Since all the eigenvalues of $A$ are positive, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is positive-definite.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

$$
\begin{aligned}{Δ}_{1} & ={a}_{11}=-3<0, \\ {Δ}_{2} & =|\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}|=2>0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, by Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x,$ and the matrix $A,$ are negative-definite.

questions.worked_solution:
Let ${Δ}_{i}$ for $i=1,2,…,n$  denote the leading principal minors of an $n\times n$ matrix $A.$ Then, according to Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is

- Statement I is false. Notice that ${a}_{11}=1,$ but 

$$

- Statement II is true, while statement III is false. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{Δ}_{1} & ={a}_{11}=1>0 \\ {Δ}_{2} & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}|=1>0 \\ {Δ}_{3} & =|A|=1>0\end{aligned}
$$

So, by Sylvester's criterion, the form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x,$ and the matrix $A,$ are positive-definite.

II. $\mathbf{x}^T \! A \, \mathbf{x}$ is indefinite

III. $A$ is positive-definite
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Given a quadratic form $Q(\mathbf x) = \mathbf{x}^T A \mathbf{x},$ we have the following theorem:

- $Q$ is positive-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are positive,

- $Q$ is negative-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are negative,

                    Identifying a Quadratic Form Type Using Sylvester's Criterion
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14169381/assets/f1a62bcd57c146902eb55f4a3a631cce69b743c9a3ff7bef659da392a5690476.svg)
Consider the matrix $A$ shown above.
Which of the following statements are true?

I. $a_{11}=-6$ and $\det(A) \lt 0$

II. $\mathbf{x}^T \! A \, \mathbf{x}$ is negative-definite

III. $A$ is positive-definite
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $\Delta_i$ for $i=1,2,\ldots,n$  denote the principal minors of an $n \times n$ matrix $A.$ Then, according to Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form $\mathbf{x}^T \! A \, \mathbf{x}$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is 

- positive-definite if and only if $\Delta_i > 0$ for all $i=1,2,\ldots,n,$

- negative-definite if and only if, for all $i=1,2,\ldots,n,$ we have $\Delta_i <          0$ when $i$ is odd, and $\Delta_i > 0$ when $i$ is even.

With that in mind, let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, $a_{11}=-6.$ Expanding $\det(A)$ along the top row, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =|\begin{aligned}-6 & -5 & 1 \\ 5 & -2 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-6)|\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}|-(-5)|\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}|+1\cdot |\begin{aligned}5 & -2 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-6)(-2)+(5)(-7)+12 \\  & =-11.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true, while statement III is false. Notice the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Δ}_{1} & ={a}_{11}=-6<0 \\ {Δ}_{2} & =|\begin{aligned}-6 & -5 \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}|=37>0 \\ {Δ}_{3} & =|A|=-11<0\end{aligned}
$$

So, by Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form $\mathbf{x}^T \! A \, \mathbf{x},$ and the matrix $A,$ are negative-definite.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

tutorials.problem:

- A quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})$ is **positive-definite** if $Q(\mathbf{x}) > 0$ for all $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{ \mathbf{0} \}.$

For example, the quadratic form

$$
S(\mathbf{x})=8x_1^2+3x_2^2
$$

is positive-definite since
$8x_1^2+3x_2^2 > 0$
for all nonzero $\mathbf{x}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14169381/assets/52e43ebb6fa34f40a73358f88aed62846332126c4fe080072c211945f54b412a.png)

- A quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})$ is **negative-definite** if $Q(\mathbf{x}) <     0$ for all $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{ \mathbf{0} \}.$

For example, the quadratic form 

$$
T(\mathbf{x})=-x_1^2-3x_2^2
$$

is negative-definite since
$-x_1^2-3x_2^2 \lt 0$
for all nonzero $\mathbf{x}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14169381/assets/a86f80966c04f960823db91bfc8711eef2bf22a81502e69b5048afc5b4799cb2.png)

- $Q(\mathbf{x}_2) <     0$ for some $\mathbf{x}_2 \in \mathbb{R}^n.$

For example, the form

$$
R(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2+2x_2^2-6x_1x_2

is indefinite. Substituting ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14169381/assets/094a61c791563994cb520b40179d77546f776bfb9148851e211ec8ed326c279a.svg) we get

tutorials.title: Introduction
tutorials.content:
In certain applications involving quadratic forms, an important question is whether a particular quadratic form $Q(\mathbf x)$ is *always* positive or *always* negative.

We classify quadratic forms using the following terminology:

- A quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})$ is **positive-definite** if $Q(\mathbf{x}) > 0$ for all $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{ \mathbf{0} \}.$

For example, the quadratic form

$$
S(\mathbf{x})=8x_1^2+3x_2^2
$$

is positive-definite since
$8x_1^2+3x_2^2 > 0$
for all nonzero $\mathbf{x}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14169381/assets/52e43ebb6fa34f40a73358f88aed62846332126c4fe080072c211945f54b412a.png)

- A quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})$ is **negative-definite** if $Q(\mathbf{x}) <     0$ for all $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{ \mathbf{0} \}.$

For example, the quadratic form 

$$
T(\mathbf{x})=-x_1^2-3x_2^2
$$

is negative-definite since
$-x_1^2-3x_2^2 \lt 0$
for all nonzero $\mathbf{x}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14169381/assets/a86f80966c04f960823db91bfc8711eef2bf22a81502e69b5048afc5b4799cb2.png)

- A quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})$ is **indefinite** if 

- $Q(\mathbf{x}_1) > 0$ for some $\mathbf{x}_1 \in \mathbb{R}^n,$ and

- $Q(\mathbf{x}_2) <     0$ for some $\mathbf{x}_2 \in \mathbb{R}^n.$

For example, the form

$$
R(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2+2x_2^2-6x_1x_2
$$

is indefinite. Substituting ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14169381/assets/094a61c791563994cb520b40179d77546f776bfb9148851e211ec8ed326c279a.svg) we get

$$
\begin{aligned}R({x}_{1}) & ={1}^{2}+2\cdot {0}^{2}-6\cdot 1\cdot 0 \\  & =1+0-0 \\  & =1>0,\end{aligned}
$$

while substituting ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14169381/assets/f4995691f0b24159baeb3cbb1ee51a9f44c72958c9288809f28f387d17b2810d.svg) we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}R({x}_{2}) & ={1}^{2}+2\cdot {1}^{2}-6\cdot 1\cdot 1 \\  & =1+2-6 \\  & =-3<0.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Positive and Negative Semi-Definite Quadratic Forms
tutorials.problem:
There are two further classifications of quadratic forms that turn out to be useful:

- A quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})$ is **positive semi-definite** if $Q(\mathbf{x}) \geq 0$ for all $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n.$

For example, the form $A(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2$ over $\mathbb{R}^2$ is positive semi-definite. Notice that this particular form is not positive-definite since it gives zero on the nonzero vector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14169381/assets/d32277694c7bd75cf76ea413fba14b25a679f84e8194c07af201e103d23a1056.svg)

- A quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})$ is **negative semi-definite** if $Q(\mathbf{x}) \leq 0$ for all $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n.$ 

For example, the form $B(\mathbf{x})=-x_1^2$ over $\mathbb{R}^2$ is negative semi-definite. Notice that this particular form is not negative-definite since it gives zero on the nonzero vector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14169381/assets/0592bc60943ac605d21672288a437282e3dddd52384b518f8869645f05540662.svg)

It's also worth noting that

- any positive-definite quadratic form is positive semi-definite, and

- any negative-definite quadratic form is negative semi-definite.

tutorials.name: Using Eigenvalues to Classify Quadratic Forms
tutorials.problem:
Given a quadratic form $Q(\mathbf x) = \mathbf{x}^T A \mathbf{x}$ with a symmetric matrix $A$,  we have the following theorem:

- $Q$ is positive-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are positive,

- $Q$ is positive semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-negative,

- $Q$ is negative-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are negative,

- $Q$ is negative semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-positive,

- $Q$ is indefinite if and only if $A$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

Using the same criteria, we can also classify the symmetric matrix $A$ as positive-definite, positive semi-definite, etc.

For example, consider the matrix $A,$ given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14169381/assets/8582c8b840b1e4696b9f83cb2c117d67e3b832e40b1ded716e0dcd23752c6f9c.svg)

Computing the characteristic equation of $A,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-5-\lambda  & -1 \\ -1 & -5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-5-\lambda )(-5-\lambda )-1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+10\lambda +24 & =0 \\ (\lambda +4)(\lambda +6) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =-4,\,-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Since all the eigenvalues of $A$ are negative, the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf x) =  \mathbf{x}^T A \, \mathbf{x}$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is negative-definite.

tutorials.title: Using Eigenvalues to Classify Quadratic Forms
tutorials.content:
Given a quadratic form $Q(\mathbf x) = \mathbf{x}^T A \mathbf{x}$ with a symmetric matrix $A$,  we have the following theorem:

- $Q$ is positive-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are positive,

- $Q$ is positive semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-negative,

- $Q$ is negative-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are negative,

- $Q$ is negative semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-positive,

- $Q$ is indefinite if and only if $A$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

Using the same criteria, we can also classify the symmetric matrix $A$ as positive-definite, positive semi-definite, etc.

For example, consider the matrix $A,$ given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14169381/assets/8582c8b840b1e4696b9f83cb2c117d67e3b832e40b1ded716e0dcd23752c6f9c.svg)

Computing the characteristic equation of $A,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-5-\lambda  & -1 \\ -1 & -5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-5-\lambda )(-5-\lambda )-1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+10\lambda +24 & =0 \\ (\lambda +4)(\lambda +6) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =-4,\,-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Since all the eigenvalues of $A$ are negative, the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf x) =  \mathbf{x}^T A \, \mathbf{x}$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is negative-definite.
